identification.title: Good and Gracious King
identification.notes: Written by Jonny Robinson, James Ferguson and Michael Farren. CCLI 7073329. CityAlight is the songwriting collective of St Paul's Castle Hill, Sydney.

claims.structuralNotes: Four verses over one repeated chorus, no bridge. Sung throughout in the first person singular and addressed to God as King. The opening verse borrows its confession from Toplady's 'Rock of Ages'.

claims.claim: The singer approaches God's throne bringing nothing of their own.
claims.subject: Approach to God

claims.claim: What the singer brings instead is a promise of acceptance from the King.
claims.subject: Acceptance

claims.claim: God is good and gracious in his rule.
claims.subject: The character of God

claims.claim: The singer rejoices precisely as one who has nothing to offer.
claims.subject: Grace

claims.claim: God is the Lord Almighty, and his kindness to the unworthy is undeserved.
claims.subject: The kindness of God

claims.claim: The singer's confidence rests on the King's character rather than their own standing.
claims.subject: Assurance

strengths.title: Arrives empty-handed and says so
strengths.explanation: The song opens by disclaiming every contribution the singer might make. That is the confession justification by faith requires, and it is made in the first line rather than buried in a later verse.
strengths.scriptureRationale: Salvation is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast — the song's opening posture.

strengths.title: Emptiness produces joy, not anxiety
strengths.explanation: Having nothing to offer is usually sung as a problem awaiting resolution. Here it is the ground of rejoicing, which is a truer instinct about how grace actually lands on a person.
strengths.scriptureRationale: Paul boasts in weakness because grace rests there — emptiness as occasion for gladness.

strengths.title: Goodness and sovereignty held together
strengths.explanation: The title puts kindness and kingship in one phrase and keeps them there for four verses. A congregation learns that God's rule and his goodness are not two facts in tension.
strengths.scriptureRationale: The Lord is gracious and merciful, and good to all — the same pairing the title makes.

strengths.title: Confidence located outside the singer
strengths.explanation: The reason the singer may approach is consistently something about the King, never something about themselves. Sustained across four verses, that is a genuine discipline.
strengths.scriptureRationale: We draw near with confidence to the throne of grace — confidence grounded in the throne, not the one approaching.

doctrinesAffirmed: The grace of God to the unworthy
theological.assessment: A disciplined song about approaching God with nothing, and its instinct is right: every reason the singer may draw near is located in the King rather than in themselves. What it never supplies is the ground of that acceptance. It borrows a hymn's confession of empty hands and answers with the King's kindness where the original answered with the cross. Sound as far as it goes, and it does not go to Calvary.

strengths.title: A hymn shape a modern room can hold
strengths.explanation: Four short verses over a single recurring chorus, with no bridge and no build. The form is old and it works: the congregation always knows where it is.

strengths.title: Survives without the band
strengths.explanation: Nothing in the song depends on the arrangement for its effect. It carries on a piano, on a guitar, or unaccompanied, which is the practical test of a congregational song.

communal.vocalRangeNote: Sung here in C, which is a comfortable congregational key. PraiseCharts publishes it in D and E flat, so C sits at or below the published range.

range.key: C (as sung here); PraiseCharts publishes D and E flat
range.note: No chart was read for this review, so the pitches are not stated. PraiseCharts does not publish a vocal range for this song.

communal.repetitionAssessment: One chorus returning after each verse, carrying the song's title claim. The repeated content is doctrinal rather than a hook, and four verses keep it from wearing thin.
communal.assessment: Written for a congregation and shaped like a hymn. Short verses, one chorus, no build to negotiate and no dependence on an arrangement.

strengths.title: Every verse lands on the same claim
strengths.explanation: Four verses approach from different angles and all resolve into the title. Nobody finishes the song unsure what it was asserting about God.

strengths.title: Old confession in current speech
strengths.explanation: The song carries hymn-weight vocabulary without archaism. It sounds like a hymn and reads like modern English, which is harder to do than it looks.

clarity.assessment: Clear in what it says and quiet about what it assumes. The words are plain and the structure is unmistakable, but the song's central adjectives rest on an argument it never makes.

synthesis.summary: A disciplined hymn-shaped song about approaching God empty-handed, with every reason for confidence located in the King rather than the singer. It borrows Toplady's confession of empty hands but answers with the King's kindness where the original answered with the cross — which is never named, nor is Christ. Sound and singable, and incomplete on its own.

scriptureReferences.relevance: The confession the opening verse makes: salvation as gift, with nothing brought.
Drawing near to the throne of grace with confidence, which is the song's whole action.
Supplies the ground of acceptance the song raises and leaves unanswered.
Pairs God's graciousness with his goodness to all, as the title does.
